Neonates of the Mongolia racerunner emerge from eggs incubated at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] after an incubation period of approximately 50 days [ab = approximately 50 days], a duration that aligns well with developmental times reported for other small-bodied lacertids from comparable thermal regimes. At the moment of hatching, these young individuals measure about 2.66 cm [Lb = about 2.66 cm] in snout–vent length and possess a wet body mass of just 0.4 grams [Wwb = 0.4 grams]. Such modest neonatal dimensions reflect a high degree of lecithotrophy; the hatchling relies entirely on residual yolk reserves during its first days of active life before transitioning to exogenous feeding. Field observations indicate that the onset of active feeding typically occurs within 24 to 48 hours after eclosion, at which point juveniles begin capturing small arthropod prey, a dietary shift that underpins the rapid somatic growth characteristic of the first growing season.

As the juvenile progresses through its first two active seasons, a sustained period of mass gain and linear elongation ensues, culminating in the attainment of sexual maturity. Under thermal conditions averaging 15 °C [T = 15 °C] during the active period, puberty, defined as the first production of viable gametes, is reached at approximately 2 years after birth [tp = approximately 2 years after birth]. This relatively extended pre-receptive interval is common among lacertids inhabiting temperate and semi-arid continental climates, where short active seasons constrain annual growth increments. For females, the onset of reproductive maturity is reflected in a mean snout–vent length of roughly 3.9 cm [Lp = roughly 3.9 cm] at puberty. This body-length threshold corresponds closely with predictions from growth models in related species and appears to be a robust indicator of functional gonadal activation across the genus Eremias.

Adult body size in the Mongolia racerunner exhibits a modest degree of sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a slightly smaller ultimate snout–vent length than males. The maximum recorded SVL in adult females is 6.58 cm [Li = 6.58 cm], whereas adult males have been documented reaching as much as 6.37 cm [Li = 6.37 cm]. Corresponding differences are also apparent in adult body mass: females reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 6.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.8 grams], while males achieve a slightly higher ultimate wet weight of about 7.0 grams [Wwi = about 7.0 grams]. These sex-specific size trajectories suggest that males may continue somatic growth for a longer period following maturation, or that energetic demands of vitellogenesis and egg production impose a growth ceiling on females.

Reproductive output in this species has been inferred from comparative data on the congener Eremias multiocellata, given the paucity of direct fecundity records for Eremias argus. At a mean active-season temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], adult females appear capable of producing up to 5 offspring per year [Ri = up to 5 offspring per year], a rate that reflects the maximum annual reproductive output under favorable conditions. This total annual fecundity likely represents multiple small clutches laid across the breeding season rather than a single large reproductive event, a pattern typical of small lacertids exploiting ephemeral insect blooms in arid steppe habitats. Unfortunately, detailed data on clutch frequency per individual female remain unavailable for this species, limiting our ability to partition the annual total into distinct nesting events.

Under field conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], longevity records for the Mongolia racerunner suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a remarkable duration for a small lacertid. This exceptional survival, relative to many temperate-zone lizards of comparable size, may be linked to the species' occupation of burrow systems that provide refuge from extreme temperature fluctuations and predation. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with reproductively active adults maintaining moderate body condition well into their eighth or ninth year. The delayed puberty, moderate output, and extended adult lifespan position Eremias argus as a relatively slow-paced species amongst the genus, a strategy presumably adapted to the unpredictability of continental steppe environments.
